Abstract 25

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) burden is rising globally, yet only subsets of patients benefit from 26

available therapies, underscoring the need for more precise molecular and cellular stratification. In the 27

PREDICT study, we enrolled treatment-naïve pediatric patients with IBD, alongside disorders of gut–brain 28

interaction (DGBI) controls and healthy donors, and profiled their intestinal and blood-derived T cells using 29

single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq). Across 107 participants, we identify a unique population of 30

cytotoxic CD4⁺ T cells (CD4 CTL) enriched in the inflamed gut of patients with Crohn's disease (CD) and 31

ulcerative colitis. CD4 CTLs are clonally expanded and express cytotoxic effector molecules and IFNG, 32

consistent with antigen-driven activation. Cell–cell interaction analyses implicate macrophage-derived IL- 33

27 as the top candidate for CD4 CTL differentiation, and IL-27 blockade in a mouse model limits CD4 CTL 34

formation. Notably, elevated CD4 CTL frequencies in gut and peripheral blood at diagnosis are associated 35

with subsequent poor outcome of anti-TNF therapy in pediatric CD. Findings in our identification cohort 36

are validated in an independent cohort and through reanalysis of published datasets. Importantly, we 37

designed a simple flow cytometry panel to isolate blood CD4+ CXCR6+ CD27- T cells, which displayed a CD4 38

CTL transcriptional phenotype. Together, our results link CD4 CTLs to anti–TNF nonresponse and support 39

their potential as an early, blood-accessible biomarker for treatment stratification in pediatric CD. 40

Keywords: Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis, TNF therapy, cytotoxic CD4 T cells 41

Introduction 42

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), which includes Crohn’s disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), is a 43

group of chronic immune-mediated disorders of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract with increasing global 44

prevalence1. Although the range of available biologic therapies to complement TNF inhibitors is improving 45

disease management, up to 50% of patients continue to exhibit primary nonresponse2,3. Currently, there 46

are no reliable biomarkers to predict treatment outcomes at diagnosis, making personalized treatment 47

strategies with approved anti-TNFs, anti-IL-12/23 pathway inhibitors, anti-α4β7 inhibitors, and JAK 48

inhibitors difficult to implement. An ideal cellular biomarker would be readily detectable in blood, 49

connected to immunopathology in the gut, and provide an actionable set of potential targets. 50

CD4⁺ T cells are central players in IBD pathogenesis. Genome-wide association studies have repeatedly 51

implicated genes involved in antigen presentation and T cell regulation, including HLA class II alleles and 52

T cell polarizing cytokine receptors such as IL23R, highlighting aberrant CD4⁺ T cell responses as key 53

genetic underpinnings of disease4-6. Functionally, CD4⁺ T cells orchestrate mucosal inflammation through 54

interactions with antigen-presenting cells, cytokine secretion, and recruitment of other effector cells, such 55

as neutrophils and inflammatory monocytes7-10. These functions depend on proper differentiation of T 56

helper subsets, which is often imbalanced in IBD, contributing to both excessive inflammation and loss of 57

immune tolerance11,12. Therapeutic targeting of TNF, IL-23 pathway, and JAK/STAT signaling further 58

reinforces the concept that T cell balance is critical to maintain gut homeostasis. Unlike classical 59

autoimmune diseases, the antigens driving T cell activation in IBD span the range from commensal 60

bacteria or fungi to viral and self-antigens, leading to a broader autoinflammatory classification13-16. 61

Despite their central role, the full heterogeneity, origins, and disease-specific functions of CD4⁺ T cells in 62

the human gut remain incompletely understood. 63

Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has recently enhanced our understanding of intestinal immune 64

dysregulation in IBD4,17-21. Prior studies have mapped cellular networks and identified pathogenic cell 65

states associated with poor treatment outcomes, such as IL13RA2⁺IL11⁺ inflammatory fibroblasts in UC22, 66

inflammatory macrophages, activated dendritic cells, plasma cells, and stromal cells in CD5, as well as 67

protective subsets like TREM2-expressing C1Qhi IL1Blo  macrophages associated with CD remission6. In the 68

same study, analysis of samples from adult patients with CD and UC before and after anti-TNF blockade 69

highlighted IFN-response signatures in T cell aggregates around epithelial damage in CD and UC, with a 70

further Th1 polarization in CD6. Our own work focusing on distinct colonic pathology in CD and UC from 71

pediatric patients reinforces the Th1- and Th17-associated T cell activation programs that correlate with 72

anti-TNF response23. However, although the Th17/IL-23 axis has yielded tractable therapeutic targets, the 73

specific effector states and pathways underlying Th1-associated pathology in CD remain less clearly 74

defined. A more refined understanding of pathogenic CD4⁺ T cell states linked to treatment outcome may 75

therefore help identify actionable biomarkers and therapeutic targets24,25. 76

To address this need, we conducted the PREDICT study, integrating scRNA-seq of intestinal biopsies and 77

peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) from treatment-naïve pediatric IBD patients, patients with 78

disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBI), and healthy donors. Here, we identify a cytotoxic CD4⁺ T cell 79

subset (CD4 CTL) enriched in both intestinal tissue and blood of CD patients, particularly those with poor 80

response to anti-TNF therapy. These CD4 CTLs appear to originate from antigen-driven clonal expansion 81

Results 86

Patient cohort and study design 87

The PREDICT study enrolled pediatric participants presenting with GI symptoms suggestive of IBD prior to 88

diagnostic workup and treatment initiation (Fig. 1A). The complete profiled PREDICT cohort included 107 89

participants. Our complete analysis cohort comprised 43 treatment-naïve patients between 6 and 19 90

years old (median 12) diagnosed with CD, 19 with UC (7–19 years old, median 13), and 28 individuals 91

without evidence of intestinal inflammation who were ultimately diagnosed with DGBI (6–21 years old, 92

median 15). DGBI patients, who exhibit GI symptoms in the absence of overt macroscopic mucosal 93

inflammation or autoimmunity, served as the primary control group for characterization of the T-cell 94

compartment. To further support our analysis, we also included 9 healthy young adult donors, 95

acknowledging their older age (18–24 years old, median 23) due to the ethical limitations of collecting 96

intestinal samples from healthy children. Eight participants classified as other diagnoses were included in 97

atlas generation and quality-control analyses but were excluded from disease-group statistical 98

comparisons. Complete clinical metadata for all participants is provided in Supplementary Table 1 and in 99

Fig. S1A-C. 100

Patients were followed for at least two years after initial endoscopy. Within the CD group, we stratified 101

patients into three categories: those who did not require biologics ("not on anti-TNF", NOA), those who 102

achieved sustained remission on anti-TNF therapy ("full response", FR), and those with partial response 103

(PR). 104

At diagnosis, we collected biopsies from the duodenum, terminal ileum, and colon, alongside PBMCs of 105

the same patients. Biopsies were separated into epithelial and lamina propria (LP) fractions, yielding a 106

total of 842 samples from 107 donors (Fig. 1B, Fig. S1A, Supplementary Table 1). In 13 donors, we 107

obtained repeated samples after the initiation of treatment. 108

Single-cell profiling and data integration 109

To characterize T-cell populations in IBD, we initially analyzed a subset of 40 participants, termed the 110

"identification cohort," using the 10x Genomics 3' scRNA-seq platform (“3p dataset”). To confirm the 111

robustness of our findings, we analyzed additional samples from an independent set of 59 donors (the 112

"validation cohort") using the 10x Genomics 5' platform (“5p dataset”), which also enabled TCR repertoire 113

analysis (Fig. 1C). For a subset of donors (n = 36), we profiled the same sample using both 3p and 5p 114

chemistries, allowing us to assess technical consistency. In such cases, donors were assigned exclusively 115

to the identification cohort for statistical evaluation. 116

First, we focused on analysis of the gut samples. In total, 283,277 T and NK cells passed quality control 117

(QC) in the 3p dataset, and 588,063 cells passed QC in the 5p dataset (Fig. 1D). We applied STACAS-based 118

integration26 over variables 10x version, sample batch and donor ID to correct for batch effects while 119

CD4⁺ Th17 cell remodeling associates with IBD and anti-TNF treatment outcome 132

To identify transcriptional differences between conditions, we performed pseudo-bulk differential 133

expression analysis using DESeq227 in the main populations of T cells and NK cells. For initial comparisons, 134

we grouped CD and UC patients into a single IBD category and compared them to non-IBD controls (DGBI 135

and healthy donors). Across cell types, the 5p dataset yielded a larger number of statistically significant 136

differentially expressed genes (DEG) than the 3p dataset, consistent with increased statistical power 137

driven by its larger cohort size (Fig. 1F, Fig. S2B). Despite these differences in DEG counts, differential 138

expression patterns were highly concordant between the 3p and 5p datasets, particularly in LP samples 139

from ileum and colon, supporting the robustness of the approach and indicating that the observed 140

signatures were not driven by cohort- or chemistry-specific effects (Fig. S2C). 141

The largest number of DEGs was observed in the CD4⁺ Th17 subset, suggesting pronounced transcriptional 142

remodeling of this subset in IBD (Fig. 1F). Among the most strongly upregulated genes in IBD CD4⁺ Th17 143

cells were those associated with proliferation (MKI67), immunoregulation (ENTPD1, encoding CD39), 144

interferon signaling (STAT1), and cytotoxicity (GZMH, GNLY, GZMB) (Fig. 1G). The acquisition of cytotoxic 145

effector gene expression within the Th17 lineage is atypical, and points to the emergence of a cytotoxic 146

program in CD4⁺ T cells in IBD, consistent with emerging literature18,20. When comparing CD patients 147

stratified by anti-TNF treatment outcome, the CD4⁺ Th17 subset again showed the highest number of 148

DEGs meeting statistical significance (Fig. 1H). This suggests that transcriptional variation within this 149

subset may contain clinically actionable biomarkers linked to therapeutic response. 150

Together, these analyses reveal that CD4⁺ Th17 cells undergo profound inflammatory and cytotoxic 151

reprogramming in pediatric IBD. While prior evidence has been limited28,29, this observation supports the 152

Th17 compartment as a central node in disease pathogenesis and treatment outcome. 153

datasets. Subclustering revealed 11 transcriptionally distinct CD4⁺ T cell subsets, which we annotated 157

Several clusters represented naïve or early memory subsets: naïve CD4⁺ T cells (clusters 1 and 2), CD4⁺ 160

Tcm (cluster 3) and naïve T regulatory (Treg) cells (cluster 5). These subsets showed a low clonal expansion 161

(Fig. 2B) and expressed canonical naïve/memory markers such as CCR7 and LEF1, with KLF2 and SELL 162

restricted to naïve cells. Activated Tregs (cluster 6) were identified by expression of FOXP3, IL2RA (CD25), 163

TNFRSF18 (GITR), and IKZF2 (HELIOS). T follicular helper (Tfh) cells (cluster 4) expressed CXCR5, CXCL13, 164

and IL21. Th2 cells (cluster 8) were characterized by GATA3, IL4 and IL5 and Th1 cells (cluster 9) expressed 165

TBX21, CXCR3 and TNF. 166

Three clusters (clusters 7, 10, and 11) shared hallmark Th17-associated genes (IL17A, IL23R, CCR6, RORC), 167

but exhibited distinct phenotypes. Cluster 7 represented classical Th17 cells, cluster 10 corresponded to 168

intraepithelial lymphocytes (IEL) and cluster 11 consisted of highly activated Th17-like cells expressing 169

PRF1, IFNG, GZMB, GNLY, and HLA-DRA, suggesting acquisition of cytotoxic function (Fig. 2C). Gene set 170

enrichment analysis (GSEA) confirmed a cytotoxic program in cluster 11 (Fig. S3E). Based on these 171

features, we identified this subset as CD4⁺ cytotoxic lymphocytes (CD4 CTL). 172

We assessed cluster enrichment by layer (epithelial vs. LP) showing enrichment of cluster 10 IELs in 173

epithelial layers and relative enrichment of classical cluster 7 Th17 and cluster 8 Th2 cells in LP layers (Fig. 174

2D). We then assessed cluster enrichment by intestinal region (e.g. duodenum vs. rest, etc.) and identified 175

relative enrichment of cluster 9 Th 1 cells in duodenum relative to other regions (Fig. 2E). 176

We hypothesized that the cluster 11 CD4 CTL population accounted for the cytotoxic gene expression 177

signature observed earlier in pseudo-bulked Th17 cells in IBD patients (Fig. 1G). To test this, we performed 178

proportionality analysis using center log-ratio transformation of cell cluster frequencies across samples30. 179

CD4 CTLs were significantly enriched in the inflamed gut of CD patients, particularly in the duodenum and 180

ileum, and in the colons of UC patients (Fig. 2F), with consistent results across both identification and 181

validation cohorts (Fig. 2G-H). 182

CD4 CTLs are reproducibly detected across cohorts and linked to anti-TNF response 183

To determine whether CD4 CTLs were also present in previously published datasets, we reanalyzed two 184

publicly available datasets: a pediatric CD cohort21 and an adult IBD cohort comprising both CD and UC 185

patients pre- and post-biologic initiation6. 186

In both datasets, we extracted and reclustered CD4⁺ T cells (Fig. S4A-B). In each cohort, we identified a 187

distinct cluster of CD4⁺ T cells expressing the same cytotoxic gene program, confirmed by an increased 188

module score calculated from the 187 top markers of the CD4 CTL cluster from the 5ʹ PREDICT dataset 189

(Fig. S4A-C). The frequency of CD4 CTLs in the two cohorts was higher in IBD patients than in healthy 190

donors (Fig. S4D-E), corroborating the findings from our cohort. Moreover, in the adult cohort, which 191

included multiple intestinal regions, CD4 CTLs were enriched across all gut regions of CD patients but only 192

in the affected gut regions (colon, rectum) of UC patients, recapitulating the disease-specific spatial 193

distribution observed in our study (Fig. S4F). 194

We next evaluated whether CD4 CTL frequencies were associated with treatment outcome in the PREDICT 195

study. In both our identification and validation cohorts, pediatric CD patients with partial response to anti- 196

TNF therapy exhibited the highest pre-treatment frequencies of CD4 CTLs in gut biopsies (Fig. 2I). In a 197

subset of patients sampled again 3–12 months after initiation of anti-TNF treatment, CD4 CTL frequencies 198

decreased in full responders, whereas in the small number of partial responders analyzed, frequencies did 199

not show an obvious decline (Fig. 2J). These findings raise the possibility that elevated CD4 CTL levels at 200

diagnosis may be associated with reduced likelihood of benefit from anti-TNF therapy. In the adult cohort 201

from Thomas et al., we do not observe significant differences in CD4 CTL frequencies before and after 202

treatment with anti-TNF, potentially indicating CD4 CTLs as an arm of the immune response that is not 203

adequately inhibited through anti-TNF blockade in persistent disease (Fig. S4G). 204

Recent work by Rios Martini and colleagues20 demonstrated that stimulation of CD4⁺ T cells from adult CD 205

patients with commensal- and food-derived yeasts induces a cytotoxic transcriptional program. We 206

hypothesized that this induced phenotype might resemble the CD4 CTLs we observed in pediatric patients. 207

Indeed, a reanalysis of their ex vivo data revealed that yeast-stimulated CD4⁺ T cells from CD patients— 208

but not from healthy donors—acquired a transcriptional profile similar to our CD4 CTL subset, including 209

robust upregulation of cytotoxic effector genes (GZMB, GZMH, GNLY, IFNG, PRF1) and characteristic 210

cytokines and receptors (IL26, IL23R, IL12RB2) (Fig. S4H-J). Out of the three yeast lysates tested, S. 211

cerevisiae induced the strongest CD4 CTL phenotype, indicating a potential environmental trigger for CD4 212

CTL differentiation (Fig. S4K-L). 213

TCR repertoire analysis reveals clonal expansion of CD4 CTLs 214

In the 5p PREDICT dataset, we combined gene expression profiling with V(D)J repertoire sequencing to 215

assess the clonality of the CD4 CTL subset. In patients with CD and UC, the most expanded clones were 216

found within CD4 CTLs, Th17 cells, and activated Tregs. In contrast, healthy donors and DGBI patients 217

showed higher clonal expansion of Th2 cells and IELs (Fig. 3A–B). 218

We next examined whether cells sharing the same TCR clonotype were confined to a single transcriptional 219

cluster or distributed across multiple CD4⁺ T cell subsets. Most expanded CD4 CTL clonotypes were 220

composed almost exclusively of cells mapping to the CD4 CTL cluster, indicating limited cross-cluster 221

overlap. In a subset of cases, however, cells from the same clonotype were also detected in Th17 or IEL 222

clusters, suggesting a potential developmental relationship between these states (Fig. 3C). Analysis of 223

clone distribution across gut regions showed that identical clones were detected in the duodenum, ileum, 224

and colon (Fig. S5A–B). We did not observe substantial clonal sharing between patients, with the 225

exception of two clones each shared across five participants (Fig. S5C). 226

associated with increased clonal expansion, supporting the biological relevance of the inferred trajectories 231

(Fig. S6A). To formally test differences in trajectory progression and fate selection, we applied the 232

Development of CD4 CTLs is orchestrated by transcription factors 248

Cytotoxicity in CD4 T cells has been associated with defined transcription factors (TF), including Runx3, 249

Eomes, Tbet (TBX21), GATA-3, Bhlhe40, Aiolos (IKZF3), and Eos (IKZF4)18,34-38. We assessed both TF 250

expression and TF activity using downstream target signatures curated in the CollecTRI database39. CD4 251

CTL (cluster 11) displayed high expression of TBX21, ID2, BHLHE40, and RORC, a pattern shared with Th17 252

(cluster 7) and IEL (cluster 10) subsets (Fig. 3F). In contrast, CD4 CTL uniquely expressed ZEB2, RUNX1, 253

STAT1, EOMES, and RBPJ, indicating the activation of a transcriptional program distinct from other CD4 254

lineages. 255

Although there was partial overlap in TF expression profiles between CD4 CTL, Th17 cells, and IELs, TF 256

activity inferred from target gene modules was entirely distinct in CD4 CTL. The most active TFs inferred 257

in CD4 CTLs included regulators of the Th1 lineage (STAT1, STAT4, TBX21, RELA), regulators of the Th17 258

lineage (RORC, STAT3, HIF1A, BATF), and TFs classically associated with CD8 T-cell cytotoxicity (EOMES, 259

RUNX3) (Fig. 3G). The combined activity of these programs accounted for the defining features of CD4 260

CTL, including simultaneous expression of Th1 cytokines, Th17 cytokines, and cytotoxic molecules. 261

Integration of transcription factor activity and gene expression across pseudotime trajectories suggested 262

that CD4 CTLs are transcriptionally related to Th1- and Th17-associated states while additionally engaging 263

a cytotoxic program (Fig. 3H). Although these analyses do not establish a definitive developmental path, 264

they support the view that CD4 CTLs represent a distinct effector state combining features of Th1, Th17, 265

and cytotoxic differentiation that are relatively terminally differentiated. Together, the clonality and 266

transcription factor activity data place CD4 CTLs in close relationship to Th1/Th17-associated CD4⁺ T cell 267

programs, while distinguishing them as a separate cytotoxic state. 268

Cytokine and cellular interactions associated with CD4 CTL development 269

Given the unusual transcriptional regulation of CD4 CTL, we next asked which cell–cell interactions and 270

local microenvironmental cues might drive their development. To address this, we integrated scRNA-seq 271

data from ileal LP across three datasets (PREDICT 3p22, PREDICT 5p, Thomas et al. 20246), this time 272

including all major lineages rather than restricting the analysis to T cells (Fig. 4A, Fig. S7A–B). After 273

integration and QC, we obtained a dataset of 1,013,968 high-quality cells spanning nine major lineages: T 274

cells, B cells, endothelial cells, epithelial cells, mast cells, myeloid cells, plasma cells, proliferating cells, 275

and stromal cells, each defined by established marker genes (Fig. S7C). 276

We further subclustered each lineage into fine-grained subsets (Supplementary Table S2) and asked 277

which populations showed the strongest correlation in abundance with CD4 CTL across samples and 278

datasets. The top-scoring populations were CD4 Treg, which—similar to CD4 CTL—were markedly 279

expanded in IBD, and two myeloid subsets: inflammatory monocyte-derived macrophages and IFN- 280

activated macrophages (Fig. 4B). The prominence of myeloid subsets in this analysis is notable, as these 281

cells are well positioned to provide both antigen presentation and instructive cytokine signals to CD4 CTL. 282

Of note, absorptive enterocytes and intestinal stem cells were negatively correlated with CD4 CTL 283

abundance, suggesting a link between CD4 CTL accumulation and epithelial remodeling in inflamed tissue. 284

We then applied ligand–receptor interaction analysis using NicheNet40 across all three datasets to identify 285

candidate ligands predicted to interact with CD4 CTLs in IBD. Consistently, we observed strong inferred 286

activity of IFN-γ, IL-27, and type I IFN signaling (Fig. 4C). IL27 and type I IFN ligands were predominantly 287

expressed by myeloid subsets, whereas IFNG was mainly expressed by T cells (Fig. 4D). IFN-γ and type I 288

IFN have been firmly linked to CD pathogenesis41, whereas the role of IL-27 is more complex: in CD4 T 289

cells, IL-27 can promote regulatory features but is also a potent driver of cytotoxic differentiation, making 290

it a plausible contributor to the CD4 CTL program42-47. 291

Strikingly, IL27 expression by myeloid cells was highly enriched in CD compared to DGBI controls and was 292

most pronounced in patients with partial response to anti-TNF treatment (Fig. 4E–F). In the Thomas et al. 293

dataset, we observed a similar trend: myeloid IL27 expression was higher in patients with active disease 294

compared to those in remission (Fig. 4G). Together, these data implicate a proinflammatory cytokine 295

circuit involving myeloid-derived IL-27 and type I interferons, together with T cell-derived IFN-γ, as a 296

microenvironmental program associated with CD4 CTL accumulation and treatment failure in CD. 297

We next tested whether the top candidate ligands from our ligand–receptor analysis, IL-27 and IFN-γ, 298

could induce a cytotoxic phenotype in CD4⁺ T cells activated in vitro with CD3/CD28 stimulation to mimic 299

strong TCR signaling (Fig. S8A-B). Flow cytometric analysis at 70 h revealed an increase in GZMB, IFN-γ 300

and Tbet, but not GZMA, in CD4⁺ T cells cultured with IL-27 or a combination of IL-27 and IFN-γ (Fig. S8C). 301

By contrast, IFN-γ alone did not induce these markers to a similar extent, highlighting a dominant role for 302

IL-27 in promoting this program and supporting the recent findings that CD4 CTLs can be differentiated 303

under specific polarizing conditions in vitro48. 304

Discussion 384

The immunopathologic mechanisms driving treatment resistance in IBD remain poorly understood, and 385

current therapies such as anti-TNF biologics benefit only a subset of patients. To address this, we 386

performed high-resolution single-cell transcriptomic profiling of T cells from treatment-naïve pediatric IBD 387

patients. 388

We revealed a transcriptionally unique subset of CD4+ T cells with cytotoxic phenotype marked by 389

expression of GZMA, GZMB, GNLY, PRF1, and IFNG, alongside Th1- and Th17-associated transcripts 390

including TBX21, CXCR3, CXCR6, RORC, IL23R, and IL26. These cells were clonally expanded, suggesting 391

antigen-driven activation, and were enriched in inflamed intestinal tissue from IBD patients. Their 392

localization mirrored disease distribution (ileum in CD, colon in UC), and in CD, their frequency was highest 393

in patients who subsequently showed poor response to anti-TNF therapy. Importantly, we also identified 394

the CD4 CTL subset within peripheral blood. 395

While several studies have recently reported on the T cell subsets enriched in CD and UC, a clear CD4 CTL 396

subset has not been defined in these studies4-6,21. However, when we reanalyzed two studies, we found 397

CD4 CTLs which were highly transcriptionally matched to those identified in the PREDICT cohort. The key 398

analytical step we took was to computationally isolate CD4 T cells away from NK cells and CD8 CTLs which 399

influence the relative enrichment of cytotoxic genes as markers for CD4 CTLs in this mixed analysis. CD4 400

CTLs have been reported in multiple settings including chronic viral infections, cancer, and aging37,53-60. 401

However, in IBD their origin, functional relevance, and relationship to clinical outcomes remain 402

incompletely defined. Our findings extend this emerging literature by defining a clonally expanded CD4 403

CTL state in treatment-naïve pediatric IBD and linking its abundance to subsequent anti-TNF response. 404

CD4⁺ T cells play a central role in mucosal immunity and IBD pathogenesis. In inflamed tissue, sustained 405

exposure to microbial- and dietary-derived antigens presented on MHC class II by epithelial and antigen- 406

presenting cells is thought to contribute to ongoing CD4⁺ T cell activation11,12,61. The CD4 CTLs identified 407

here combined inflammatory cytokine expression with cytotoxic effector molecules, suggesting potential 408

contributions to epithelial injury and chronic inflammation. Notably, major therapeutic classes used in 409

IBD—including anti-TNF agents, anti-integrin therapy, anti-IL-12/23, and JAK inhibitors—target pathways 410

that intersect with these effector programs62,63. Whether and how these therapies modulate CD4 CTL 411

abundance or function in the gut remains an important question. 412

The differentiation of effector CD4⁺ T cell subsets is shaped by signals from the local tissue 413

microenvironment. Through cell–cell interaction analysis of our scRNA-seq datasets from inflamed ileal 414

tissue, we found that CD4 CTL development is associated with exposure to type I and type II interferons, 415

as well as IL-27—cytokines known to promote cytotoxic T cell programs64-66. Type I interferons and IL-27 416

were predominantly expressed by myeloid cells, suggesting that these cells may serve as both antigen- 417

presenting and cytokine-producing drivers of CD4 CTL differentiation. In contrast, IFN-γ was produced 418

primarily by CD4 CTLs themselves, potentially reinforcing a self-amplifying inflammatory loop within the 419

tissue. 420

While these transcriptional interactions suggest a cytokine-driven circuit for CD4 CTL development, their 421

spatial context remains unknown. Recent spatial transcriptomics atlases of CD and UC have revealed 422

compartmentalized immune cell niches and altered cellular interactions in inflamed gut tissue67,68. Future 423

spatially resolved studies will be essential to determine the localization of CD4 CTLs within the mucosa, 424

An important unanswered question is which antigens are recognized by CD4 CTLs in IBD. Addressing 427

antigen specificity is challenging because CD4 CTLs are infrequent, current computational methods cannot 428

reliably infer specificity from TCR sequence alone, and HLA heterogeneity complicates both in silico 429

prediction and ex vivo testing. Nonetheless, recent work has reported enhanced CD4⁺ T cell reactivity to 430

yeast antigens in CD, which was associated with acquisition of cytotoxic phenotype ex vivo20. Consistent 431

with this, we identified a TCR clonotype shared between yeast-stimulated CD4⁺ T cells in that dataset and 432

CD4 CTLs from two CD patients in our cohort, where it mapped specifically to the CD4 CTL cluster. 433

Although anecdotal, this observation raises the possibility that some CD4 CTLs recognize S. cerevisiae– 434

derived antigens and supports the broader hypothesis that persistent microbial antigen exposure 435

contributes to CD4 CTL differentiation in the inflamed gut. 436

Finally, we demonstrate that CD4 CTLs are not restricted to the intestinal mucosa in pediatric CD but are 437

also detectable in peripheral blood by both scRNA-seq and flow cytometry. This supports the feasibility of 438

measuring circulating CD4 CTLs using a clinically accessible assay and identifies them as a candidate blood- 439

based biomarker for baseline treatment stratification. Furthermore, it may also provide a route for them 440

to recirculate and be recruited to distal regions of the intestine beyond the initial site of inflammation. 441

In summary, our study defines an IBD-associated cytotoxic CD4⁺ T cell state that is clonally expanded, 442

enriched at disease-relevant intestinal sites, and linked to poor response to anti-TNF therapy. Prospective 443

validation in larger and independent cohorts will be required to establish whether quantification of CD4 444

CTLs at diagnosis can support patient stratification, guide therapeutic decision-making in IBD, and whether 445

they present a subset which is causal and targetable for therapy. 446
